title: Self-Employed? Timeshare Presentation Income Rules 2026
metaTitle: Self-Employed? Timeshare Presentation Income Rules (2026) | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Yes, self-employed people can attend timeshare presentation deals. Income is rarely verified at the door; the common bar is $50K+ household income and age 25+.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Yes, self-employed people can attend timeshare presentation deals and qualify for the same discounted rates as W-2 employees. Brands almost never verify income at the door, and the common eligibility bar is a household income of roughly $50,000 or more plus age 25+. Self-employment counts as income; you generally just need a valid photo ID and a major credit card in your name.
heroImageAlt: Self-employed timeshare presentation income rules — the common bar is $50,000+ household income, rarely verified
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: Yes, self-employed people qualify for timeshare presentation deals. Income is stated, not usually documented, and the common bar across brands is a household income around $50,000+ and age 25 or older. Whether you draw a paycheck or invoice clients, you meet the requirement the same way: you attend as a qualified couple or individual with a valid ID and a major credit card.

If you run your own business, freelance, or draw income from a company you own, you may wonder whether the vacation deals that come with a resort preview are open to you. They are. The eligibility rules for a timeshare presentation were written around household income and marital status, not around how you receive that income. Across the roughly 617 deals we track, the recurring requirements are age, income, and a couples-attend-together rule, and none of them exclude the self-employed.

Can self-employed people attend timeshare presentations?

Yes, self-employed people can attend timeshare presentations and book the discounted package. The qualification screen a resort applies is designed to confirm you are a plausible buyer: of legal purchasing age, with enough household income to finance a purchase, and attending as a decision-making unit. A sole proprietor, LLC owner, contractor, or freelancer who states a qualifying household income meets that screen. When you book a package from a brand like Westgate or Wyndham, the phone or web qualification form typically asks you to confirm you meet the income threshold, not to prove how you earn it.

The reason is practical. The resort is selling you a stay in exchange for your time; the income question exists so their sales team is talking to people who could theoretically buy. Self-employed households often clear the bar easily, so brands have no incentive to turn you away.

What counts as proof of income for the self-employed?

In the vast majority of cases, nothing is checked at all. Income on a timeshare presentation deal is effectively an honor-system statement you make at booking. If a brand does ask for anything, it is usually only at check-in and usually only a photo ID and a credit card in your name to confirm you are the person who qualified. It is rare for a preview-deal desk to request a tax return, a 1099, or a profit-and-loss statement. That said, requirements vary by brand, and you should confirm at booking exactly what the resort will ask for on arrival.

Do the timeshare presentation income rules change if you are self-employed?

No. The timeshare presentation income rules apply the same dollar threshold to everyone; being self-employed does not raise or lower the bar. What sometimes trips people up is the credit card requirement rather than the income one. Because a valid major credit card in your name is a near-universal requirement, a self-employed person who runs everything through a business debit card should bring a personal credit card to check-in. The income you state should be your total qualifying household income.

Key fact: About 47% of the vacation deals we track openly disclose a required preview presentation, and among those the average disclosed session runs about 116 minutes. Income is part of the qualification screen for those deals, but it is stated, not audited, in nearly every case we see.

How to book a presentation deal when you are self-employed

Book exactly as any other traveler would. Choose a package, confirm you meet the age and income bar during the qualification step, and bring a photo ID plus a personal credit card to check-in. If you want to compare current offers, browse our full list of vacation deals or a specific market like Orlando or Las Vegas, where entry-level packages regularly start near $49. For the full picture on how the income bar differs across companies, see our Income Requirement Index, which compiles the requirement across every brand we cover.

The bottom line for self-employed travelers: your income structure is not a barrier. State a qualifying household income, bring the right ID and card, and you have the same access to these deals as anyone else. When you are ready, check the latest verified prices on our rate recap and grab a package that fits your dates.

title: Retired Couples & Timeshare Presentations: Who Qualifies
metaTitle: Retired Couples & Timeshare Presentations: Who Qualifies | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Yes, retired couples qualify for timeshare presentation deals. Pension and Social Security income counts toward the ~$50K bar; a few brands set upper age caps.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Yes, retired couples qualify for timeshare presentation deals in most cases. Pension, Social Security, annuity, and investment income all count toward the common household-income bar of roughly $50,000. The main catch is that a minority of brands enforce an upper age cap, so confirm the age policy at booking.
heroImageAlt: Retired couples timeshare presentation eligibility — pension and Social Security income counts toward the $50K bar
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: Yes, retirees qualify for presentation deals. Retirement income — pension, Social Security, annuities, IRA and 401(k) draws, and investment income — counts toward the common household-income requirement of about $50,000. The one thing to check is age: most brands only set a minimum age (commonly 25+), but a small number set an upper cap, so confirm the age policy before you book.

Retired couples are, in many ways, the ideal audience for a timeshare preview: time to travel, discretionary income, and a taste for repeat vacations. So it surprises people to learn that a handful of brands quietly apply an upper age limit. The good news is that qualifying on income is straightforward for most retirees, and the age question is easy to clear up with one phone call at booking.

Do retirees qualify for presentation deals?

Yes, retirees qualify for presentation deals as long as they meet the income and age bars. The household-income requirement — commonly around $50,000 combined — does not distinguish between a salary and a pension. Social Security, a defined-benefit pension, annuity payments, and regular draws from retirement accounts all count. Because income is almost always stated at booking rather than documented, a retired couple simply confirms they meet the threshold during the qualification step, the same as a working couple booking a Wyndham or Westgate package.

What retirement income counts toward the requirement?

All regular household income counts. When a brand asks whether your household earns at least the threshold, you may include every recurring source, not just wages. That typically means the following:

Pension / annuityYesCounts as recurring income

Investment / rental incomeYesPart of household income
Part-time / consultingYesAdds to the total
 General pattern across tracked presentation deals; income is stated, not audited, in nearly every case — confirm at booking. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

Do age caps exist for timeshare presentations?

Yes, upper age caps exist at a minority of brands, though most only publish a minimum age. Where an upper cap appears, it is usually tied to the resort's financing model — a developer may be reluctant to write a long-term timeshare loan for a much older buyer. These caps are not universal and are not always disclosed on the booking page, so the safe move is to ask directly: "Is there any maximum age to attend and qualify for this rate?" If a cap applies to one brand, another brand in the same market almost always has no cap. Because policies vary by brand, treat any specific cap you hear as something to confirm at booking rather than a fixed rule.

Key fact: Age minimums are far more common than maximums. The typical floor across the deals we track is 25+, with some brands at 21, 28, or 30. Upper caps exist but are the exception, not the rule — and they differ by brand and even by resort within a brand.

Booking tips for retired couples

Two practical notes. First, both members of a married or cohabiting couple are expected to attend the presentation together; a retiree traveling without a spouse should read our guide on attending without a spouse first. Second, bring a major credit card in your name — this is a near-universal requirement regardless of age. Retirement-friendly markets like Branson and Orlando carry some of the lowest entry prices we track, often near $49 to $59.

One more practical point for retirees: because you likely have flexible dates, you can aim for shoulder-season windows when preview inventory is widest and prices sit at the bottom of their range. Retirement-heavy markets such as Branson and Gatlinburg frequently post their lowest entry rates midweek and outside peak holiday weeks, so a couple with an open calendar can often beat the average price a working household would pay. Keep a valid credit card and matching-ID handy, confirm the age policy once, and the qualification is genuinely quick.

If you want the definitive requirement-by-requirement breakdown before you book, our Income Requirement Index lays out the income bar across every brand we cover, and you can compare live offers on the full vacation deals list. Retirement is arguably the best season for these packages — just confirm the age policy and the rest follows easily.

title: Attending a Timeshare Presentation Without Your Spouse
metaTitle: Attending a Timeshare Presentation Without Your Spouse | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Most brands require couples to attend together, so attending a timeshare presentation without your spouse is often not allowed. The rules and workarounds.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Usually no — most timeshare presentation deals require married or cohabiting couples to attend together, so one spouse showing up alone can void the promotional rate. A single, unpartnered traveler is treated differently and can often attend solo. If you are partnered but your spouse cannot come, call the brand before you travel, because policies vary and some will accommodate you.
heroImageAlt: Attending a timeshare presentation without your spouse — most brands require both partners to attend together
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: If you are married or living with a partner, most brands require both of you to attend the presentation together, and one spouse attending alone can forfeit the discounted rate. If you are genuinely single with no partner, you are usually allowed to attend solo. When your spouse simply cannot make the session, call the resort in advance — some will let you attend alone by exception, but you should never assume it.

This is one of the most misunderstood rules in the whole vacation-deal world. The "both must attend" clause is not about being married on paper; it is about getting both decision-makers of a household in the room at the same time. Understanding why the rule exists tells you exactly when it applies to you and when it does not.

Can one spouse attend a timeshare presentation alone?

Usually not, if you are a couple. Nearly every brand that requires a preview writes the rate around a rule that both spouses or both members of a cohabiting couple attend the presentation together. If you booked a couple's rate and show up without your partner, the resort can decline to honor the promotional price or reschedule you. The reason is straightforward: timeshare purchases are typically joint household decisions, and the sales team does not want to pitch one half of a couple who will say "I have to ask my spouse." So the requirement is really about who is in the room, not your marital paperwork.

Which brands enforce the both-attend rule?

Most do, to varying degrees of strictness. The requirement is close to universal in principle, but enforcement varies by brand and even by resort. Some verify at check-in and turn away a solo-arriving partner; others are more flexible if you call ahead. Because the specifics differ, the table below describes the common pattern rather than promising any one brand's policy.

Your situationCommon ruleCan you attend without them?
Married couple, joint rateBoth must attend togetherUsually no; call ahead to ask
Cohabiting couple, same addressBoth must attend togetherUsually no; treated like spouses
Genuinely single travelerSolo attendance often allowedYes, but may face a solo surcharge
Spouse unable to travelCase-by-case exceptionSometimes, only if pre-approved
 General industry pattern; enforcement varies by brand and resort — confirm at booking. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

What workarounds are actually allowed?

The only reliable workaround is to disclose your situation before you travel and get an exception in writing or by confirmed phone call. If your spouse cannot attend, tell the reservations line at booking and ask whether you can attend the presentation alone at the quoted rate. Some brands will accommodate a documented reason; others will offer to rebook you for dates when both can attend. What does not work is booking a couple's rate, showing up alone, and hoping no one notices — that is the scenario most likely to cost you the discount or trigger a rack-rate charge. If you are single, you are not working around anything; you are simply booking as a solo traveler, which our guide to single travelers and presentation deals covers in detail.

Key fact: The both-attend rule is about household decision-makers, not marriage certificates. That is why an unmarried couple sharing an address is usually held to the same standard as a married one — see our page on unmarried couples.

How to book with confidence

It also helps to understand what "attend together" means on the day. Both partners generally need to be present for the full presentation and to sign in at the start; ducking out early or having one partner arrive late can be treated the same as not attending together. If a genuine emergency separates you mid-trip, tell the resort's front desk immediately rather than skipping the session, because a documented, communicated problem is handled very differently from a silent no-show. Planning for both of you to complete the tour together is the single simplest way to protect your rate.

Before you buy any package, decide honestly whether you are attending as a couple or as a single traveler, then book to match. If you are a couple and there is any chance one partner cannot attend, resolve it at booking, not at the check-in desk. For live prices, check the rate recap and book dates that work for both of you.

title: Unmarried Couples at Timeshare Presentations: The Rules
metaTitle: Unmarried Couples at Timeshare Presentations: The Rules | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: You usually don't have to be married to attend a timeshare presentation, but most brands require a cohabiting couple attending together. How the rules work.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: No, you generally do not have to be married to attend a timeshare presentation deal. Most brands require a couple that lives together and attends together, not a marriage certificate. The common test is cohabitation and both partners present, sometimes with matching-address ID; specifics vary by brand, so confirm at booking.
heroImageAlt: Unmarried couples at timeshare presentations — cohabitation, not marriage, is the common requirement
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: You do not need to be married to attend a timeshare presentation deal. Most brands ask for a cohabiting couple that attends together, which they interpret as two partners who live at the same address and are both present at the session. A few brands may ask for matching-address ID; many ask for nothing beyond both partners showing up. Rules vary by brand, so confirm the specifics when you book.

The word "married" appears in a lot of forum posts about vacation deals, but it rarely appears in the actual requirement. What brands are really screening for is a household — two people who could jointly buy a timeshare — not a legal marriage. That distinction is good news for unmarried couples, and it is worth understanding precisely so you are not caught off guard at check-in.

Do you have to be married to attend a timeshare presentation?

No, you do not have to be married to attend a timeshare presentation. The common requirement is a cohabiting couple that attends together, and "cohabiting" simply means you live together as partners. Brands use this framing because their goal is to pitch a household's joint decision-makers. A long-term unmarried couple satisfies that goal exactly as well as a married one. When you book a package with a brand like Westgate or a broker offering a Wyndham preview, the qualification screen typically asks that you attend as a couple, not that you produce a marriage license.

How are cohabitation clauses decoded?

A cohabitation clause is the brand's way of saying "a real couple who lives together." In practice it is enforced loosely. The most a brand usually does is ask both partners to attend and, occasionally, to present ID. The table below shows how the common requirement maps to what unmarried couples actually experience.

 General industry pattern; matching-address checks are occasional and vary by brand — confirm at booking. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

What about same-address proof?

Same-address proof is the strictest form of the cohabitation rule, and it is the exception rather than the norm. Where a brand does check, it usually means glancing at two IDs and expecting the addresses to match, or accepting a simple statement that you live together. If your IDs list different addresses — common for couples who have not updated a license or who keep separate legal residences — call the brand before you travel and ask how they handle it. Many will accept the couple's rate anyway; a strict one may ask for a piece of shared mail. Because this varies by brand, treat address matching as something to confirm at booking, not a universal hurdle.

Key fact: The both-attend rule and the cohabitation rule are two sides of the same coin: brands want both household decision-makers in the room. If one partner cannot attend, read our guide on attending without a spouse first.

Booking as an unmarried couple

It is worth knowing why the cohabitation framing exists rather than a strict marriage test. Timeshare products are sold as long-term household commitments, and an unmarried couple who share finances and a home is exactly the kind of buyer developers want in the room. That is why the requirement centers on living together and both attending, not on a certificate. It also means the rule is applied with common sense: a couple who can plainly present as partners rarely faces scrutiny, while the friction only appears in edge cases like mismatched ID addresses, which a quick call resolves.

Book as a couple, plan for both of you to attend, and bring photo ID plus a major credit card. If your IDs show different addresses and you are worried, a two-minute call at booking clears it up. Compare live offers across popular couple markets like Orlando, Las Vegas, and Cancun on our full vacation deals list, and see how the income side works on the Income Requirement Index. For unmarried couples, the rules are simpler than the internet suggests: live together, attend together, and you qualify.

The credit card requirement causes more confusion than any other part of a vacation deal, mostly because two different things get blurred together: the card as an eligibility signal and the card as security for a hold. Separating them makes the whole thing clear and removes the worry that you are being charged for a discounted package you already paid for.

Why do timeshare presentation deals need a credit card?

Presentation deals need a credit card for two reasons: it is a soft signal that you are a plausible buyer, and it gives the resort security for a hold. A major credit card in your name suggests you have established credit and could finance a purchase, which is part of why brands like Westgate and Wyndham ask for one. Just as importantly, the card lets the resort place a refundable authorization hold to cover incidentals or to enforce the requirement that you actually attend the presentation. It is not a purchase and, in the normal case, you are not charged.

How much is held on your card?

The hold amount varies widely by brand and resort, from a modest incidentals authorization to a larger no-show deposit. Are debit cards accepted?

Often not for the hold. It also helps to know how the hold interacts with your available credit. An authorization does not charge you, but it does reduce the spending room on your card for as long as it sits open, which can matter if you plan to use the same card for meals, activities, or a rental car during the trip. If your limit is tight, either bring a second card for daily spending or ask the resort to place the hold on one card and let you pay incidentals on another. Checking your card issuer's app after checkout confirms the authorization has dropped off, and if it lingers longer than the quoted window, a quick call to the resort or issuer clears it.

Before you book, ask three questions: Is a hold placed, how much, and when is it released? Bring a major credit card in your name with enough available credit to cover the hold on top of your normal spending. Then simply complete the presentation and check out on time, and the hold reverses. Bottom Line Up Front: Your credit score generally does not determine whether you can attend a timeshare presentation deal. Brands rarely run a hard credit check just to let you book the discounted stay; what they want is a valid major credit card in your name. A credit pull usually only happens if you choose to finance an actual timeshare purchase during the presentation, which you are never obligated to do.

People often confuse two very different moments: qualifying to attend a presentation, and applying for financing to buy a timeshare. They have completely different credit implications. Once you separate them, the worry about your score mostly disappears — attending is the easy part.

Do timeshare presentation deals run a credit check?

Usually not, just to attend. To book and attend a presentation deal, brands typically ask for a valid major credit card and confirmation that you meet the age and income bars. That card requirement is not the same as a credit check; the resort is confirming you hold established credit, not scoring your file. A formal credit inquiry normally only happens later, if you sit through the presentation and decide to finance a purchase. So for the discounted vacation itself — the reason you are booking a Westgate or Wyndham package — your score is not the gatekeeper.

Soft pull vs hard pull: what is the difference?

A soft pull is a background check that does not affect your score and may happen without a formal application; a hard pull is a full inquiry that can ding your score a few points and requires your consent. For presentation-deal eligibility, neither is typically required beyond presenting a card. If you later apply for developer financing to buy, that is where a hard pull comes in. How to book without worrying about your score

There is one more reassurance worth stating plainly: the sales pressure during the pitch does not translate into a hidden credit consequence. Even if a representative runs illustrative numbers or asks about your finances to tailor an offer, that conversation is not the same as a formal credit application, and no inquiry hits your report unless you sign a financing agreement and authorize the pull. You can engage with the presentation, ask questions, and still walk away with zero impact to your score. The only decision that touches your credit file is a deliberate one you make to finance a purchase, and you retain full control over whether that ever happens.

title: The Cooldown Rule: How Often You Can Do Each Brand
metaTitle: The Cooldown Rule: How Often You Can Do Each Brand | VacationDeals.to
metaDescription: Most brands limit how often you can book a discounted timeshare presentation deal, commonly a 6, 12, or 24-month cooldown per brand. Here is how the rule works.
author: The VacationDeals.to Team
bluf: Most brands limit how often the same household can book a discounted presentation deal, commonly a 6, 12, or 24-month cooldown per brand. The rule is tied to your name, address, and sometimes phone number, and it usually resets per brand — so a cooldown at one brand rarely blocks you at another. Confirm the exact window at booking, since it varies.
heroImageAlt: Timeshare presentation cooldown rule — commonly 6, 12, or 24 months per brand before you can rebook
content:
Bottom Line Up Front: Brands cap how often you can take a promotional presentation deal, most often a 6, 12, or 24-month cooldown per brand and per household. The clock is tracked by your name, address, and sometimes phone number, and it typically resets separately for each brand. That means a cooldown with one brand usually does not stop you from booking a different brand right away. Windows vary — confirm yours at booking.

The cooldown rule exists because these deals are a marketing cost: the resort subsidizes your stay hoping to pitch you once. They do not want to keep subsidizing the same household that already declined. Understanding how the window is tracked tells you exactly when you can book again and how travelers legitimately stack deals across brands.

How often can you attend the same brand's presentation?

You can typically take a given brand's discounted presentation deal once per cooldown window, most commonly every 6, 12, or 24 months. After you attend, that brand flags your household as having used a promotional rate, and you generally cannot book their subsidized deal again until the window passes. This is why the same person can enjoy a Westgate deal now and a Wyndham deal next month — different brands, separate clocks. The cooldown protects the brand's marketing spend, not the entire market.

What do the 6, 12, and 24-month windows look like?

The window length is a brand choice and is not always published, so treat the following as the common pattern rather than a fixed rule for any one company.

24 monthsStricter brandsHousehold record

 General industry pattern; exact windows vary by brand and are not always disclosed — confirm at booking. Source: VacationDeals.to, July 2026.

What happens if you double-dip early?

If you try to book the same brand's promotional rate before the cooldown ends, the most common outcome is that the reservation is flagged and declined, or you are quoted the standard price instead of the deal. Because the brand matches on your name, address, and sometimes phone, using slightly different contact details to slip through is the kind of misrepresentation that can get a booking canceled at check-in. The clean approach is to wait out the window or simply book a different brand, which is entirely allowed. Our guide on existing owners covers the related rule for people who already own with a brand.

Key fact: Cooldowns are per brand, not per industry. Across the 35 brands and 80 destinations we track, that leaves plenty of room to legitimately book a new deal from a different company while one brand's clock runs down.

How to plan around the cooldown

It is worth being clear about what the cooldown does and does not restrict, because travelers often overestimate it. The window applies only to a brand's subsidized promotional rate — it does not stop you from booking that same resort at its standard published price, staying as a regular guest, or booking an entirely different brand's preview deal in the same city on the same dates. In other words, the cooldown protects one specific discount, not your access to travel. Frequent vacation-deal users treat it as a simple rotation schedule: note the date and brand of each promotional stay, and let the calendar tell you when that particular deal is available to you again.

Keep a simple record of which brand you last booked and when, then rotate to a different brand for your next trip. If you love a particular resort, note its cooldown window and rebook once it clears. You can line up your next deal from a different brand across markets like Orlando and Las Vegas on the full vacation deals list, and check the eligibility landscape on our Income Requirement Index. Rotating brands is how frequent travelers keep the cheap stays coming without breaking any rule.

Bottom Line Up Front: Owning a timeshare does not lock you out of these deals — it just changes which ones you qualify for. Preview rates are aimed at prospective first-time buyers, so you typically cannot take a preview deal with the brand you already own. You can generally still book preview deals with other brands, and your current brand may offer you an owner-update rate instead. Rules vary, so confirm at booking.

A lot of existing owners assume the whole world of vacation deals is closed to them. It is not. The only door that reliably closes is the preview deal at your own brand, and even that has an alternative. Once you understand the difference between a preview deal and an owner update, the map is simple.

Can existing owners book preview deals?

Existing owners can usually book preview deals with brands they do not already own, but not with their current brand. Preview rates are a customer-acquisition tool: the resort subsidizes your stay to pitch you a first purchase. If you already own with them, you are not a prospect for that pitch, so their preview deal typically excludes you. But you are a fresh prospect to every brand you do not own — so an owner of one company can book a preview deal from another, such as moving between a Westgate stay and a Wyndham preview, subject to each brand's own rules.

Owner-update vs preview: what is the difference?

An owner update is a presentation aimed at people who already own with the brand, usually to sell more points or an upgrade, and it often comes with its own discounted stay. A preview deal is aimed at non-owners. They can look similar from the outside — a cheap stay in exchange for a presentation — but they are different tracks with different audiences and pitches.

Are there cross-brand loopholes?

The main legitimate path is simply booking preview deals with brands you do not own — that is not a loophole, it is how the system is designed. Where owners get into trouble is trying to book their own brand's preview rate by omitting that they are an owner; brands match on your name and address and can catch it at check-in, costing you the rate. If your current brand offers an owner-update stay, that can be a genuinely good deal on its own terms. And because preview cooldowns are tracked per brand, an owner of one company still has many other brands available — see our guide to the cooldown rule for how those clocks work.

Key fact: Being an owner narrows your options at exactly one brand — your own. Across the 35 brands and 80 destinations we track, the rest of the market is still open to you as a first-time prospect.

How owners should book

Existing owners sometimes worry that a brand will "see" their other-brand ownership and decline them, but that is rarely how it works. Brands generally match against their own customer records, not a shared industry database of every timeshare you hold, so owning with one company is usually invisible to another. What a brand does check is whether you already own with them specifically. This is why the honest, simple strategy — book a preview deal with a company you do not own, and let your current brand pitch you an owner update separately — works cleanly and keeps every rate you book fully valid at check-in.

Be upfront about what you own, then aim your preview-deal booking at a brand you do not own. If your current brand pitches you an owner-update stay, weigh it as its own offer rather than assuming it is off-limits. Ownership changes your options; it does not end them.

Most vacation-deal marketing pictures a couple, which leaves single travelers unsure whether the offers even apply to them. They often do — but with wrinkles around pricing and income that are worth understanding before you book, so you are not surprised by a surcharge or a couples-only rule at the desk.

Can singles book couple-priced deals?

Sometimes, but not always at the same price. Many preview deals are built and priced around a couple, because the sales team wants both household decision-makers present. A single traveler can frequently still book, but the brand may apply a solo surcharge, ask for a higher individual income to offset the missing second earner, or in some cases restrict the promotional rate to couples entirely. So the honest answer is that a single can often attend, yet should not assume the exact couple's headline price will apply. When you see a low Orlando or Las Vegas rate, check whether it is quoted per couple before you count on it as a solo price.

How do solo surcharges work?

A solo surcharge is the brand's way of recovering value when only one person attends the pitch. It can show up as a higher package price, a higher income threshold for a single qualifier, or a supplement added at booking. Because the couple-priced headline rate is what most marketing shows, a single traveler who reads it as their own price can be disappointed, but one who asks about solo terms up front often finds a brand that genuinely welcomes them at a fair rate. Solo-friendly properties tend to be those that value filling a room and a presentation seat over the exact composition of the household, and they exist in every major market. Accessibility questions come up often and rarely have a scary answer: resorts are hospitality businesses used to accommodating guests, and the presentation is just a meeting in one of their rooms. The key is timing — a request made in advance is far easier to fulfill than one sprung at the sales desk. This page is informational and describes common practice, not a legal ruling on any specific brand's obligations.

Are timeshare presentations wheelchair accessible?

Yes, timeshare presentations are generally held in wheelchair-accessible spaces, since they take place in resort meeting rooms, sales galleries, or conference areas that are typically part of an accessible property. If accessible parking, a step-free route, or particular seating matters to you, mention it at booking so the resort can route you correctly on the day. Accessibility on the vacation itself — an accessible room, roll-in shower, and so on — is a separate request you make the same way. What about ASL interpreters and other accommodations?

Reasonable accommodation applies to the sales session the same way it applies to the rest of the stay, so if you need to sit rather than tour a model unit on foot, take a break, or have materials presented in a format you can access, you can ask for that and expect a reasonable effort to meet it. A good-faith request does not weaken your position or obligate you to buy anything; you retain the same right as any attendee to complete the session and decline. Framing your needs clearly and early lets the resort prepare, and it keeps the focus where it belongs — on a comfortable, accessible vacation.
